stops.name: Backshell
stops.text: artist’s depiction of the aeroshell containing the lander separating from the orbiter – credit NASA Viking’s aeroshell provided protection for the lander during its entry into Mars’ atmosphere. The aeroshell consisted of two parts, the backshell and the heat shield. As it approached and entered the atmosphere, thrusters on the backshell controlled the attitude of the aeroshell. In addition to the frictional braking from the heat shield, the aeroshell’s angle of attack provided lift which helped slow the spacecraft’s descent. The backshell included instruments to study the upper atmosphere of Mars. At an altitude of 6,400 meters, a mortar in the backshell fired, deploying a parachute. The lander slowed and descended under the parachute to an altitude of 1,200 meters, at which time the lander separated from the backshell and parachute to make the final descent on its thrusters. Years later, the HiRISE camera aboard the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter was able to image the backshell a short distance to the west of the lander. The parachute seems to be visible draped just to the south of the backshell.

stops.name: Parachute
stops.text: Artist’s depiction of parachute being deployed from the backshell – credit NASA Viking’s aeroshell provided protection for the lander during its entry into Mars’ atmosphere. The aeroshell consisted of two parts, the backshell and the heat shield. As it approached and entered the atmosphere, thrusters on the backshell controlled the attitude of the aeroshell. In addition to the frictional braking from the heat shield, the aeroshell’s angle of attack provided lift which helped slow the spacecraft’s descent. The backshell included instruments to study the upper atmosphere of Mars. At an altitude of 6,400 meters, a mortar in the backshell fired, deploying a parachute. The lander slowed and descended under the parachute to an altitude of 1,200 meters, at which time the lander separated from the backshell and parachute to make the final descent on its thrusters. Years later, the HiRISE camera aboard the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter was able to image the backshell a short distance to the northwest of the lander. The parachute may possibly be visible draped just to the southeast of the backshell.

stops.name: Lander
stops.text: Viking Lander – credit NASA The three-legged, 450 kilogram lander featured communications antennae, two scanning cameras, a seismometer, and a mast supporting meteorology instruments. A robotic arm included a sample scoop, a temperature sensor, a magnet, and mirrors to provide views of otherwise inaccessible areas. Viking biology experiments included the Pyrolytic Release experiment, the Labeled Release experiment, and the Gas Exchange experiment. A gas chromatograph/mass spectrometer measured the composition and abundance of organic compounds in the Martian soil and the composition of the Martian atmosphere. An x-ray fluorescence spectrometer was used for inorganic chemistry analysis. The lander was also equipped with computer, power, data, and thermal control systems. Power was supplied by radioisotope thermoelectric generators. After descending to 1,200 meters on its parachute, the lander jettisoned the parachute, extended its 3 legs, and made the final descent to the surface using its terminal descent thrusters which fired for 40 seconds to slow the final velocity to 2 meters per second. The nearly featureless terrain of the landing site prevented pinpointing the lander’s location by comparing ground-based images from the lander with images from orbiters. stops.name: Heat Shield
stops.text: Artist’s depiction of heat shield protecting the aeroshell and lander during atmospheric entry – credit NASA Viking’s aeroshell provided protection for the lander during its entry into Mars’ atmosphere. The aeroshell consisted of two parts, the backshell and the heat shield. The heat shield protected the lander from the intense heat of entry into Mars’ atmosphere and provided frictional braking. After the parachute was deployed from the backshell at a height of 6,400 meters, the heat shield was discarded, falling to the ground. The heat shield’s final location northeast of the lander was identified years later when it was imaged by the high-resolution HiRISE camera aboard the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.

stops.name: Heat Shield
stops.text: Viking Heat Shield – credit NASA Viking’s aeroshell provided protection for the lander during its entry into Mars’ atmosphere. The aeroshell consisted of two parts, the backshell and the heat shield. The heat shield protected the lander from the intense heat of entry into Mars’ atmosphere and provided frictional braking. After the parachute was deployed from the backshell at a height of 6,400 meters, the heat shield was discarded, falling to the ground. The heat shield has tentatively been identified as a dark feature northeast of the lander in an image by the high-resolution HiRISE camera aboard the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.

stops.name: Pathfinder Lander
stops.text: View from lander after successful entry, descent and landing. During descent and at an altitude of 355 meters, a cluster of airbags was inflated, surrounding and protecting the lander. At an altitude of 21.5 meters, the lander separated from the backshell, falling and then bouncing in its encasing balloons to a rest on the ground, where the balloons were deflated. This successful entry, descent, and landing strategy became the model for the future MSL rovers. The lander opened it petals revealing solar panels and the Sojourner rover. The lander conducted imaging and meteorology studies, and acted as a communications relay for the Sojourner rover. NASA honored the legacy of Dr. Carl Sagan by renaming the lander the Carl Sagan Memorial Station.

stops.name: Parachute
stops.text: Artist rendition of parachute deployment. After the heat shield had slowed Pathfinder to about 1,300 kph (830 mph), the backshield deployed the parachute, which slowed Pathfinder to a velocity of 245 kph (153 mph). Pathfinder rode the parachute down to an altitude of 98 meters at which point the backshell’s retrorockets were fired.

stops.name: Backshell
stops.text: Pathfinder's aeroshell with its three retrorockets firing. Pathfinder’s aeroshell provided protection for the lander and rover during its seven-month journey to Mars and its entry into Mar’s atmosphere, and consisted of two parts, the heat shield and the backshell. The backshell contained the parachute, a tether for lowering the lander and rover, various electronics, and three retrorockets. Once the heat shield had slowed Pathfinder to about 1,300 kph (830 mph), the backshell jettisoned the heat shield, deployed the parachute and lowered Pathfinder down the 20-meter tether. At an altitude of 98 meters, the backshell fired its retrorockets, slowing Pathfinder to a velocity of 0 at an altitude of 21.5 meters. The rover and lander then detached from the backshell falling to the ground. This successful entry, descent, and landing strategy became the model for the future MSL rovers.

stops.name: Heat Shield Debris
stops.text: Artist rendition of heat shield upon entry into Mars' atmosphere. Pathfinder’s aeroshell provided protection for the lander and rover during its seven-month journey to Mars and its entry into Mar’s atmosphere, and consisted of two parts, the heat shield and the backshell. The heat shield protected the rover and lander from the intense heat of entry into Mars' atmosphere, slowing them from 22,000 kph (13,600 mph) down to about 1,300 kph (830 mph), and was then jettisoned shortly after the parachute opened.

stops.name: Sojourner Rover
stops.text: Sojourner rover on the surface of Mars. The first robotic rover to drive on the surface of Mars, Sojourner’s instrumentation included three cameras and an Alpha Proton X-ray Spectrometer (APXS) to measure composition of Martian rocks and dust. Designed for a mission lasting 7 sols (Martian days or 24 hours, 39 minutes, and 35.244 seconds), but actually continued operating for 83 sols, until a battery in the lander finally was exhausted. During that time, it covered a distance of 100 meters around its landing site.

stops.name: Columbia Memorial Station
stops.text: Spirit rover One of two robotic rovers in NASA's Mars Exploration Rover program, Spirit was designed to explore the geology of Mars, look for evidence for the presence of liquid water on Mars' surface in the past, look for geological clues to the environmental conditions that existed when liquid water was present, and assess whether those environments were conducive to life. Spirit's landing site was named Columbia Memorial Station in honor of the seven astronauts killed in the Space Shuttle Columbia disaster.

stops.name: Bonneville Crater
stops.text: Panorama view of Bonneville crater After departing from its landing site, Spirit drove along the rims of Bonneville crater (200 meter diameter, 10 meter depth), Missoula crater (91 meter diameter, 18 meter depth) and Lahontan crater (55 meter diameter, 9 meter depth) as it drove along the floor of Gusev crater. During this initial stage of its journey, Spirit found no signs of lake deposits. Instead, the ground was covered in basaltic lava rock that showed only slight signs of alteration by very small amounts of water. If a lake floor had been there, it had been covered by later deposits of volcanic rock.

stops.name: Pot of Gold
stops.text: A rock that researchers named "Pot of Gold" NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory directed Spirit toward the Columbia Hills, a range of low hills on the floor of Gusev crater, about 3 kilometers from Spirit's landing site. These hills are composed of older material rising above the volcanic debris surrounding it. As Spirit climbed into the hills, the mineralogy around it changed. A rock that researchers named "Pot of Gold" was found to contain the mineral hematite, which often forms in the presence of water. The amount of olivine in rocks around Spirit declined as the amount of sulfates went up, and increasing "Pot of Gold" at close view concentrations of phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine, and bromine were measured - all consistent with the rocks having been in the presence of water. Discovery of the mineral Goethite was important, since it forms only in the presence of water.

stops.name: Husband Hill
stops.text: The View from Husband Hill on Mars. Credit: Mars Exploration Rover Mission, Cornell, JPL, NASA Perhaps the best vantage point for Spirit to survey the terrain it was exploring came when it climbed to the top of Husband Hill, the tallest of the Columbia Hills. Not only did Husband Hill provide an expansive vista, it also provided some excellent rock outcrops to study. The Cumberland Ridge on Husband Hill was examined in detail by Spirit. The presence of the mineral goethite here showed that water had been involved in the formation of these rocks. Rock here was also found to have a higher concentration of phosphorus than had been seen anywhere on Mars before. One possibility explaining the high phosphorous levels could be phosphate deposited by water.

stops.name: Comanche Outcrop
stops.text: Comanche Outcrop on Mars indicates hospitable past In March, 2005, while driving downhill from its exploration of Husband Hill and McCool Hill, Spirit came upon a rock outcrop scientists named Comanche. Analysis of Comanche with Spirit’s spectrometers showed Comanche to be very carbonate rich. Carbonates form in the presence of water, and the water they form in cannot be very acidic. Later analysis of data from Spirit by a team led by Steve Ruff at Arizona State indicated that this carbonate formed in low temperature surface water, consistent with a lake in Gusev crater.

stops.name: Silica Valley
stops.text: Bright white silica-rich material revealed from a stuck rover wheel. While driving in the Columbia Hills in March, 2006, the front right of Spirit’s 6 wheels stopped turning. Turning around and dragging the stuck wheel behind it resulted in a fascinating discovery. At one point, the stuck wheel scraped away the dark surface soil revealing bright white silica-rich material below. This material formed either in a hot spring or steam fumarole, either of which might possibly have provided an environment suited for microbial life.

stops.name: Home Plate
stops.text: Spirit's View Beside 'Home Plate' Credit: JPL, NASA Within the Columbia Hills, Home Plate is a plateau about 90 meters across. It was picked out from orbit as a high priority target for Spirit to explore. Analysis using the instruments aboard Spirit indicated that Home Plate may have been formed from deposits resulting from a hydrovalcanic explosion. Basaltic magma rising through the rock may have encountered subsurface briny water. The heat of the magma turned the water into high-pressure steam, resulting in an explosive eruption.

stops.name: Troy
stops.text: View of Spirit's traverse and location of it's final communication. On May 1, 2009, Spirit became stuck in soft soil at the western edge of Home Plate. The ground team tried repeatedly to free the rover from its trap, but on January 26, 2010, NASA declared that Spirit was now a stationary research station. During previous Martian winters, Spirit was able to park on sunward-facing slopes to maximize power to its solar cells in order to survive the winter. But now that it was stationary, it was no longer able to perform this tactic. The final communication with Spirit occurred on March 22, 2010. During its lifetime, it traveled more than 7.7 kilometers across the Martian surface. It functioned for 2,210 Martian days, far beyond its original primary mission of 90 Martian days (a Martian day lasts for 24 hours, 39 minutes, and 35.244 seconds). During this time, Spirit returned fascinating clues to Mars’ watery past.

stops.name: Landing Site
stops.text: The martian landscape at Meridiani Planum, Opportunity's landing site. Opportunity’s journey across Mars’ surface has included stops at several impact craters. These craters expose multiple layers of bedrock, allowing Opportunity to read the history recorded in these layers of rock. As luck would have it, Opportunity actually landed in a small impact crater. Eagle crater, with a diameter of 22 meters and a depth of 3 meters, proved to be an excellent place for Opportunity to start its mission. The crater contains exposed rock outcrops which, upon close examination, revealed the source of the grey hematite readings seen from space. “Blueberries” (hematite spheres) on a rocky outcrop at Eagle Crater. In the rock and ground around it are numerous small, hematite-rich spherules which the scientists referred to as “blueberries”. The blueberries are actually concretions that formed in the presence of water. Opportunity’s journey across Mars’ surface has included stops at several impact craters. stops.name: Eagle Crater
stops.text: Eagle crater with Opportunity lander as seen by Opportunity rover Opportunity’s journey across Mars’ surface has included stops at several impact craters. These craters expose multiple layers of bedrock, allowing Opportunity to read the history recorded in these layers of rock. As luck would have it, Opportunity actually landed in a small impact crater. Eagle crater, with a diameter of 22 meters and a depth of 3 meters, proved to be an excellent place for Opportunity to start its mission. The crater contains exposed rock outcrops which, upon close examination, revealed the source of the grey hematite readings seen from space. In the rock and ground around it are numerous small, hematite-rich spherules which the scientists referred to as “blueberries”. The blueberries are actually concretions that formed in the presence of water.

stops.name: Endurance Crater
stops.text: Endurance crater as seen by Opportunity rover After leaving Eagle crater, scientists at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory directed Opportunity on a journey that took it to Endurance crater (130 meter diameter, 20 meter depth). Upon arrival at the crater, it was obvious that the crater exposed layers of stratified rock. A survey conducted from the rim found a safe entry point from which to drive Opportunity into the crater. Study of the layers of exposed rock showed the complexity of the history of water in this area with the region having apparently been flooded on multiple occasions, with dry periods in between. At the floor of Endurance Crater is a field of sand dunes, which the rover team chose to avoid so as to minimize the risk of getting the rover stuck. After spending over six months inside Endurance Crater, Opportunity exited safely and continued its journey across Meridiani Planum.

stops.name: Heat Shield
stops.text: The remains of the heat shield from Opportunity, broken into two pieces. After leaving Endurance Crater, the rover team directed Opportunity to the site of the impact of its heat shield. Engineers were excited about the chance to examine the shield to evaluate its performance in protecting Opportunity from the roughly 1,000-degree Celsius temperatures as it entered Mars’ atmosphere. An iron meteorite, the first meteorite to be found on another planet. This task was found to be more challenging than initially thought when Opportunity found the shield, broken into two main pieces, had inverted, or turned itself inside out upon impact with the ground.In a fascinating coincidence, a basketball-sized nickel-iron meteorite was found to be lying on the surface next to the heat shield. This was the first meteorite to be found on another planet. Opportunity spent 36 sols (Martian days) at this site.

stops.name: Victoria Crater
stops.text: Victoria crater as seen by Opportunity rover At 750 meters in diameter and 70 meters in depth, Victoria Crater is significantly larger than either Eagle or Endurance craters. When Opportunity arrived at the crater, it drove about a quarter of the way around the rim, mapping the crater and looking for a safe route in. Again, numerous layers of sedimentary rock were exposed and a large dune field occupied the floor of the crater. Inside the crater, analysis of the exposed rock showed that the processes that had been at work locally in Eagle and Endurance craters acted more widely, on a regional scale. Sulfate salts were produced by the interaction between basalt rock and acidic water. Sand generated, transported, and deposited by the wind became cemented into sedimentary rock under the influence of groundwater. Differences between layers told how the processes of sedimentary rock formation changed as Mars became more arid. Opportunity spent 341 sols (Martian days) exploring inside Victoria Crater before exiting and continuing on.

stops.name: Endeavour Crater
stops.text: Endeavour crater as seen by Opportunity rover A long journey brought Opportunity to the edge of Endeavour Crater. At 22 kilometers in diameter and 300 meters deep, it is by far the largest crater that Opportunity will examine. During its exploration along the rim of the crater, Opportunity came upon a vein of calcium sulfate, probably in the form of gypsum, protruding up above the surrounding rock. Color view of the mineral vein called "Homestake" from Opportunity's panoramic camera. This vein, named Homestake, probably formed from water dissolving calcium out of volcanic rocks and then combined with sulfur either leached from the rock or from volcanic gas. This deposit tells a story of water that was far less acidic (and possibly more hospitable to life) than was found in previous locations. Additional sulfate veins were encountered as Opportunity continued its journey along the rim toward an area known as Marathon Valley which measurements from orbit indicate is rich in phyllosilicate clay minerals, rich in clues to Mars’ watery past.

stops.name: Homestake
stops.text: Opportunity looking out to the plains where its backshell (left) and parachute (right) landed. While traversing north along the Cape York area of Endeavour Crater’s rim, Opportunity came upon a vein of calcium sulfate, probably in the form of gypsum, protruding up above the surrounding rock. This vein, named Homestake, probably formed from water dissolving calcium out of volcanic rocks and then combined with sulfur either leached from the rock or from volcanic gas. This deposit tells a story of water that was far less acidic (and possibly more hospitable to life) than was found in previous locations. Additional sulfate veins were encountered as Opportunity continued its journey along the rim toward Marathon Valley.

stops.name: Matijevic Hill
stops.text: Matijevic Hill panorama – credit NASA / JPL-Caltech / Cornell / Arizona State University Venturing south along the eastern slopes of Cape York on Endeavor Crater’s west rim, Opportunity circled and explored a feature that would become known as Matijevic Hill. Data from the Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars (CRISM) onboard the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) indicated that tis area should be rich in smectite clay minerals that had formed in the presence of water. In a rock unit they called Whitewater Lake at Matijevic Hill, Opportunity came upon rich deposits of smectite clays including nontronites and montmorillonite, providing new evidence of a time on Mars when water flowed and life might possibly have emerged. Matijevic Hill was named for Jake Matijevic, one of the original members of the MER design team and former chief of MER engineering.

stops.name: Ulysses Crater
stops.text: Comet Siding Spring as imaged by Opportunity – credit NASA/JPL-Caltech/Cornell Univ./ASU/TAMU After leaving the Cape York area, Odyssey headed south along the west rim of Endeavour Crater toward Marathon Valley. Along the way, it stopped to examine a small crater named Ulysses Crater and the blanket of pulverized rock ejected around it. From here, on Sol 3817 of its mission (Oct. 21, 2014), Odyssey used its Panoramic Camera to image Comet Siding Spring, which passed only 139,500 kilometers from Mars, far closer than any previous recorded flyby of a comet past Mars or the Earth.

stops.name: Marathon Valley
stops.text: Marathon Valley panorama – credit NASA / JPL-Caltech / Cornell / Arizona State University Marathon Valley cuts through the western rim of Endeavor Crater. It attracted the interest of researchers because data from the Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars (CRISM) onboard the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) indicated that tis area should be rich in smectite clay minerals that had formed in the presence of water. Researchers thought they might find rich clay deposits there similar to those they found around Matijevic Hill. Instead, they found that the iron-rich clay is mixed throughout the area with bedrock that was broken and ejected in the impact that formed Endeavour. Deep red bands crossing the valley indicated fractures where water may have flowed, altered existing rock, and deposited soluble minerals. Examination of these bands did not reveal smectites, but did find magnesium sulfate, something researchers would expect to find precipitating from water. After exploring Marathon Valley, Opportunity exited back out the western opening of the valley and continued south in its exploration of Endeavour Crater.

stops.name: Spirit Mound
stops.text: Spirit Mound (NASA / JPL-Caltech / Cornell / ASU). After more than a terrestrial year of exploring Marathon Valley, Opportunity exited the valley on Sol 4482 through Lewis and Clark Gap heading to the east, downslope and inward, along the rim of Endeavour Crater. As Opportunity continued across the terrain of Cape Tribulation, the name giving to this raised section of the crater’s western rim containing Marathon Valley, the rover team guided the rover to a hill dubbed Spirit Mound. The team had thought they might possibly find ancient Matijevic Formation material there, similar to what they had found earlier in Cape York. But upon arriving at the Spirit Mound, they found more of the brecciated rocks of the Shoemaker Formation that they had become quite familiar with in their traverse across Cape Tribulation.

stops.name: Rocheport
stops.text: Striated rock formation at Rocheport (NASA / JPL-Caltech / Stuart Atkinson). After leaving Spirit Mound, Opportunity headed southwest up and outward along the raised section of Endeavour Crater’s rim known as Cape Tribulation. The goal was to exit Cape Tribulation and head south along the Meridiani Plain, to the next raised section known as Cape Byron. Cresting the rim, Opportunity reached a gap named Rocheport on Sol 4640, where it would finally exit Cape Tribulation. Taking a farewell pan of the terrain revealed a section of striated Shoemaker Formation bedrock that appeared to have been etched or carved by something. Opportunity made a final stop in this region to examine the striated rock. Possible explanations for the striations included formation by ice, wind erosion, or a spillover of water. Discussion continued as Opportunity journeyed on, leaving Cape Tribulation behind.

stops.name: Cape Byron
stops.text: Entrance to Perseverance Valley (NASA / JPL-Caltech / Cornell / ASU / Seán Doran). After leaving Cape York behind, Opportunity made excellent time going south across the smoother terrain of the Meridiani plain on its way to Cape Byron, the next segment of the raised rim of Endeavour Crater. The main goal at Cape Byron was to explore Perseverance Valley, a fluid-carved gully cutting down across the rim of the crater. Perseverance seems to be Noachian in age, dating back to when Mars had its most abundant amount of surface water and was perhaps at its most habitable state. In targeting Perseverance Valley, researchers wanted to determine if the valley was in fact carved by water. If so, they planned to examine flow features and sediments to determine of how it was formed, perhaps carved by a river, spillover from a lake, or a wet debris flow. In making the traverse down the gully, researchers looked forward to encountering more exposures of ancient Matijevic Formation material, similar to what they had found earlier in Cape York, and exiting the gully deeper into Endeavour than they have been yet. Transit of Phobos in front of the Sun captured with Opportunity’s Pancam (NASA / JPL-Caltech / Cornell / ASU / Texas A&M). Opportunity reached the top of Perseverance Valley on Sol 4718, allowing it to be at the right place at the right time to view Mars’ moon Phobos transit across the

stops.name: La Bajada
stops.text: On Sols 4720 and 4721, the robotic geologist kept its astronomer hat on and captured two more solar eclipses by Phobos. Opportunity then spent the next 60 Sols exploring the region just above Perseverance Valley, and scouting a route down the valley, making observations from promontories on the north and south sides of the valley’s head. Then, on Sol 4781 (July 6, 2017), Opportunity proceeded down into Perseverance Valley. View down Perseverance Valley. Credit NASA / JPL-Caltech / Cornell / ASU / Sean Doran Its pace down the valley was slowed by the deep cold of the local Martian winter as well as a communications blackout that occurred while Earth’s and Mars’ orbits positioned them on opposite sides of the Sun. In the beginning of November, 2017 Opportunity was in an area that had been labeled as “La Bajada”. The area was characterized by two differing rock outcrops coming together. The northern outcrop exhibited what appeared to be small, etched erosional tails that seemed to indicate scouring in an uphill direction. Opportunity was positioned over a good example site dubbed Mesilla from Sols 4890 through 4906. Study with the Pancam, Microscopic Imager (MI), Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer (APXS) confirmed these as wind-carved erosional features. La Bajada. Credit NASA / JPL-Caltech / Cornell / ASU

stops.name: The Island
stops.text: Continuing on from La Bajada, Opportunity made its way to a point roughly half way down Perseverance Valley. On January 1, 2018, it stood at the western end of a rock formation that split the valley into two forks. From Sols 4934 – 4957, the two forks were imaged and studied from the tip of the dividing formation, given the name “The Island”. It was decided to explore the northern fork first. Opportunity proceeded up the fork to examine a formation dubbed “Nueva Vizcaya” on the north wall of the fork. Opportunity operated there during Sols 4993-4996, taking detailed measurements of the outcrop. It then turned back south and made its way back to the western tip of The Island. It was there that Opportunity reached a remarkable milestone, marking Sol 5000 on the surface of Mars. This was an amazing achievement, especially considering the rover’s original 90-Sol specification! Opportunity was now poised to explore the south fork of Perseverance Valley Opportunity at Nueva Vizcaya. Credit NASA / JPL-Caltech

stops.name: Backshell and Parachute
stops.text: Opportunity looking out to the plains where its backshell (left) and parachute (right) landed. Opportunity’s aeroshell provided protection for the rover during its seven-month journey to Mars and its entry into Mars’ atmosphere, and consisted of two parts, the heat shield and the backshell. The heat shield protected the rover and lander from the intense heat of entry into Mars’ atmosphere, slowing them from 12,000 mph down to 1,000 mph, and was then jettisoned shortly after the parachute opened at 30,000 feet. The backshell contained the parachute, a tether for lowering the lander and rover, various electronics, and three retrorockets. The rover and lander detached from the backshell about three seconds before landing. Opportunity drove to the heat shield’s impact location. While it did not visit the backshield or parachute, it did image them from the edge of Eagle Crater.

stops.name: Heat Shield
stops.text: Phoenix’s aeroshell provided protection for the rover during its seven-month journey to Mars and its entry into Mars’ atmosphere, and consisted of two parts, the heat shield and the backshell. The heat shield protected the lander from the intense 1,400° C (2,600° F) heat of entry into Mars’ atmosphere, slowing it from 21,000 kph (13,000 mph) down to 1,400 kph (900 mph). At that point, at an altitude of 12.6 km (7.8 miles), the parachute was designed to open and, shortly afterward, the head shield was jettisoned.

stops.name: Phoenix Lander
stops.text: Artist rendition of Phoenix lander. The Phoenix lander’s objectives were to study the history of water on Mars in all its phases, and to search for evidence of a habitable zone and assess the biological potential of the ice-soil boundary. The presence of this ice was confirmed when it was exposed in a trench dug by Phoenix’s robotic arm. Findings of soil analysis from the area revealed the presence of carbonates as well as perchlorate. Phoenix also observed snow falling from clouds above it. Designed to operate for three months, Phoenix lasted for five months before succumbing to the diminishing light of the approaching winter. The advancing winter ice cap covered the area, with later images from orbit the showing the remains of the spacecraft after the ice had retreated.

stops.name: Parachute
stops.text: Phoenix hanging from its parachute as it descended to the Martian surface. Phoenix’s parachute, contained in the backshell, was designed to be deployed after the heat shield had slowed Phoenix to 1,400 kph (900 mph), at an altitude of 12.6 km (7.8 miles). The deployment of the parachute occurred about seven seconds later than planned, but Phoenix landed successfully within the targeted area. Phoenix rode the parachute down to an altitude of 1 km (3,200 ft) and a velocity of 200 kph (125 mph) before separating from the backshell, and making the final descent using its rocket engines. Phoenix’s descent by parachute was captured from orbit by the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.

stops.name: Backshell
stops.text: Artist rendition of backshell with Phoenix exposed. Phoenix’s aeroshell provided protection for the rover during its seven-month journey to Mars and its entry into Mars’ atmosphere, and consisted of two parts, the heat shield and the backshell. The backshell contained the parachute, and a wraparound antenna to transmit an ultra-high frequency signal to Earth via NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) or Mars Odyssey spacecraft. At an altitude of 1 km (3,200 ft) and still falling at 200 kph (125 mph) Phoenix separated from the backshell, freefalling for about half a second before firing its rockets for its final descent to the surface.

stops.name: Bradbury Landing
stops.text: Goulburn rock outcrop: conglomerated fluvial sediment at Bradbury Landing Bradbury Landing is the landing site for the Curiosity rover within Gale Crater. It is named after writer Ray Bradbury and is located in Aeolis Palus, a flat plain between Gale Crater's northern rim and central peak. Aeolis Palus lies in what appears to be the wash debris of Peace Vallis, an outflow channel flowing down the slope of Gale Crater's rim. Shortly after landing, Curiosity found evidence supporting this view in the form of rock outcrops in the immediate area composed of conglomerated fluvial sediments, the type of formation that would form in a vigorously flowing stream.

stops.name: The Rocknest
stops.text: 'Rocknest' From Sol 52 Location Leaving Bradbury Landing, Curiosity drove east across the plain of Aeolis Palus. Between the rover’s 55th and 100th sols on Mars (a sol is a Martian day, 24 hours, 39 minutes, and 35.244 seconds), Curiosity stopped in a sand pit that became known as the Rocknest. At this location, Curiosity used its scoop and ChemMin X-ray diffraction analyzer to perform its first soil analysis on Mars. In these tests, Curiosity found abundant, easily accessible water at 1.5 to 3 weight percent.

stops.name: Glenelg
stops.text: Yellowknife Bay area of Glenelg. NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS Continuing eastward, Curiosity spent over 200 sols in a region known as Glenelg. This area marks a junction of 3 different terrain types and provided Curiosity with the opportunity to examine bedrock that was being exposed as the wind eroded the overlying mudstone. At Glenelg, in a shallow depression known as Yellowknife Bay, Curiosity made use of its drill to obtain samples from mudstone sedimentary rock formations that were named John Klein and Cumberland. The trip to Glenelg was a significant detour for Curiosity on its journey to Mt. Sharp. But it was selected for investigation because previous observations from orbit by the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and other spacecraft indicated that water had played a major role in forming rock deposits here. The detour turned out to be worth it. Curiosity’s investigations at Glenelg demonstrated that Gale Crater was indeed the site of a lake in the distant past, that water was there at multiple times, and that sometimes the water was flowing and sometimes it was still. Mass spectrometry measurements by Curiosity obtained an age of four billion years for a sample of rock that had been deposited on the lakebed and showed that it had been uncovered by wind erosion about 80 million years ago.

stops.name: Darwin Outcrop
stops.text: Darwin Outcrop with Mt. Sharp in the background. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech After leaving Glenelg, Curiosity turned southwest on its long journey to the slopes of Mt. Sharp. Along the way, researchers had identified several interesting areas of rock outcrops that would serve as waypoints for scientific investigation along the way. The first of these, Darwin Outcrop was visited by Curiosity from sols 392-396. The sandstone outcrop contained pebbles rounded and deposited by flowing water. Later, intrusive veins of water-related minerals penetrated cracks in the sandstone. Findings at Darwin Outcrop broadened the area demonstrated to have been altered by flowing water, and continued to reveal the complex history of water on Mars.

stops.name: The Kimberly
stops.text: Curiosity selfie at the Windjana drilling site. NASA/JPL-CALTECH (EDIT BY DOUG ELLISON/JPL) From sols 581 to sol 630, Curiosity examined a complex area of outcrops named the Kimberly. This formation consists of three distinct units. Three peaks mark the topmost unit. Beneath them is a smooth-textured unit. Below that is a striated unit. A location named Windjana, on the southeast foot of the southern peak in the Kimberly was the site for Curiosity’s next drilling operation. The Kimberly, Curiosity rover, and its tracks imaged by the HiRISE camera on MRO, Credit: NASA/JPL/University of Arizona As seen from orbit, the Kimberly seemed to offer interesting similarities to what was found if the Yellowknife Bay area of Glenelg. Specifically, researchers were looking for comparisons with areas of scarp retreat in Yellowknife Bay, where a top layer of mudstone is being eroded from the rock beneath. While similar structures were visible at the Kimberly, a key difference was that in the Kimberly, Curiosity encountered sandstone rather than mudstone.

stops.name: Pahrump Hills
stops.text: Pahrump Hills outcrop and surrounding terrain. NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS On sol 753 of its mission, Curiosity arrived at the base of Mt. Sharp. The foothills at the base of the mountain here are named the Pahrump Hills. These are part of the Murray formation, which underlies all of the other exposed rock layers of Mt Sharp. Researchers expect that this represents the oldest geological unit that Curiosity will encounter in its journey. Within the Pahrump Hills, Curiosity drilled at three sites, Confidence Hills (sol 759), Mojave (sol 882), and Telegraph Peak (sol 908). At the Mojave site, a preliminary analysis indicated the presence of jarosite, which would point to rock forming in more acidic water that was found in previous sites, and further illustrate the variety in the history of water on Mars. While at the Pahrump Hills, Curiosity took some time to point its cameras up from the rocks below it to observe the comet Siding Spring as it passed closer to Mars than any comet has passed to Earth in recorded history. On sol 923, Curiosity left the Pahrump Hills by way of Artist’s Drive Valley, continuing its exploration at the base of Mt Sharp. From here, Curiosity will continue to traverse into younger layers of sedimentary rock, reading the history of how the environment of Mars and the habitability on Mars changed over time.

stops.name: Marias Pass
stops.text: Marias Pass with older mudstone (center) in contact with overlying sandstone – credit NASA/JPL/MSSS Leaving the Pahrump Hills and continuing southwest, Curiosity made its way to Marias Pass. This region marks the transition between two very different rock units. The Murray formation, which includes the Pahrump Hills is composed of mudstone presumably deposited on a lake floor. Above it is the Stimson formation which formed from wind-deposited sand. Drilling into Murray formation rock just below Marias Pass on Sol 1060, Opportunity obtained samples of a silica mineral called tridymite. This was surprising, since tridymite is formed in association with explosive silicic volcanism that is common on Earth, but rare or even unknown on Mars. Its presence may force scientists to rethink the volcanic history of Mars. Studying the transition between Murray and Stimson rock layers, researchers found that millions to maybe even hundreds of millions of years elapsed between the formation of these two layers. Continuing its drive onto the washboard surface of Stimson terrain, Curiosity’s cameras revealed bright halos surrounding fractures in the rock. These bright halos were found to be enriched in silica compared to surrounding rock.

stops.name: Bagnold Dunes
stops.text: Curiosity self-portrait on the edge of Namib Dune in the Bagnold Dunes – credit NASA/JPL/MSSS After driving across the rough, washboard surface of Stimson sandstone, Curiosity reached the edge of the Bagnold Dunes on Sol 1174. Extending northeast to southwest, this active dune field features wind-driven dunes whose movement can be seen from orbit in MRO’s HiRISE camera. Ever since Curiosity’s landing, the Bagnold dunes have presented a barrier between the rover and its goal of the higher slopes of Mt. Sharp. Carefully advancing to the edge of the dune field, Curiosity sampled the sand and then continued southwest staying off the edge of the sand.

stops.name: Bagnold Dunes West End
stops.text: Curiosity self-portrait on the Naukluft Plateau – credit NASA/JPL/MSSS By Sol 1368, Curiosity had driven to the western reaches of the Bagnold Dunes. All along, the Curiosity team had been mindful of the hazards of sand, and how Spirit’s mission ended when it became stuck in sand in the Columbia Hills. But now, after a long westward drive along the Naukluft Plateau off the north edge of the dunes, a clear path was available for Curiosity to ascend the slopes of Mt Sharp to the south. Curiosity turned left and began heading south and up toward the Murray Buttes.

stops.name: Murray Buttes
stops.text: Mastcam mosaic showing cross-bedded sandstone layers in one of the Murray Buttes (NASA/JPL/MSSS/Ken Kremer/kenkremer.com/Marco Di Lorenzo). After rounding the western edge of the Bagnold Dudes, Curiosity continued south to the Murray Buttes. The mudstone of the Murray Formation that Curiosity has been traversing tells a story of alternating flooding and drying of the ancient lakebed in Gale Crater. The Murray Buttes tell a story of one of the dry periods in this area. They are composed of layered, cross-bedded sandstone originally deposited by wind as migrating sand dunes. The buttes are spectacular landmarks leading south and up the slope of Mt Sharp. Looking ahead from here, the rover team targeted the hematite-rich Vera Rubin Ridge, a clay-rich unit above that, and a sulfate-rich unit even further up. But while still in the Murray formation, Curiosity continued to drill and sample until a fault in the drill feed mechanism disabled the drill on Sol 1536.

stops.name: Bagnold Dunes South
stops.text: “Curiosity Navcam image of linear dunes in southern segment of Bagnold Dunes (NASA/JPL-Caltech). After leaving the Murray Buttes behind, Curiosity skirted a southern extension of the Bagnold Dunes. This dune field was noticeably different from what Curiosity had encountered in the north. The northern dune field was characterized by arc-shaped barchan dunes indicating that the wind typically blows north to south in that area. But in the southern dune field, the dunes were linear in shape. Researchers suspected that these could be seif dunes, which could indicate frequently changing wind direction.

stops.name: Vera Rubin Ridge
stops.text: Fine layering revealed in this Remote Micro-Imager mosaic of Vera Rubin Ridge (NASA/JPL-Caltech/LANL/CESR) On Sol 1741, Curiosity was looking across a small patch of sand at the base of Vera Rubin Ridge. From this vantage, Curiosity’s Remote Micro-Imager provided stunning views of fine layering in the face of the ridge. This raised ridge is about 200 meters wide and extends about 6.5 kilometers from northeast to southwest, approximately parallel to the Bagnold Dunes. Observations from orbit using the CRISM spectrometer aboard the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter revealed the ridge to be rich in the mineral hematite. This iron oxide mineral forms in association with water, and close study of this deposit could be very useful in understanding the history of water in Gale Crater. Detailed examination by Curiosity could help determine what chemical processes were involved in the formation of the hematite, providing valuable clues about the environment at the time the deposits formed, and the potential for habitability for life at that time. From this location, the rover team planned to drive Curiosity east along the base of the ridge toward a safe location where the rover could climb onto the ridge.

stops.name: Top of Vera Rubin Ridge
stops.text: Curiosity continued to the southeast along the base of Vera Rubin Ridge searching for a slope shallow enough for it to make the climb up to the broad, flat crest of the ridge. Along the way, it studied the transition from the now-familiar mudstone of the Murray Formation at the ridge’s base to an array of new rock types on the face of the ridge above. On Sol 1796, Curiosity turned south and headed toward an accessible-looking rock ramp heading up the ridge. It started climbing up the ridge’s flank, and on Sol 1809, it made the transition to driving up the bedrock of Vera Rubin Ridge. Climbing onto Vera Rubin Ridge on Sol 1809. Credit NASA / JPL / Sean Doran The ascent to the top of the ridge took several Sols. On the way up, the rover paused to examine fascinating purple and tan exposures of rock. On Sol 1814, Curiosity’s Navcam returned spectacular panoramas from the flat expanse at the top of the ridge. The rover’s ascent path had taken it to one of the large fractures crisscrossing the area. Researchers were eager to examine the fracture to look for any signs if it might have once been a conduit of water through the rock. Nearing the top of Vera Rubin Ridge on Sol 1812. Credit NASA / JPL / MSSS / Paul Hammond

stops.name: Hematite Hotspot
stops.text: After climbing to the top of Vera Rubin Ridge, Curiosity proceeded south across the width of the broad flat ridgetop. It then turned northeast to continue its exploration of the ridge. Throughout this investigation, the rover remained hampered by a non-functioning drill. Along the way, engineers devised a way to operate the drill using the using pressure from the arm to press the drill into the rock instead of using the broken drill feed mechanism. Two attempts at drilling holes this way were made on Sols 1977 and 1984. While both attempts succeeded in drilling holes, the rock proved to be too hard to go deep enough to get retrievable samples. Curiosity continued northeast along the ridgetop and on Sol 2004 was positioned on top of what measurements from orbit indicated was the strongest concentration of hematite anywhere along the rover’s planned path. This iron oxide mineral typically forms in association with water. High concentrations of hematite measured from orbit were the motivation for exploring the ridge. Multispectral measurements from Curiosity’s Mastcam confirmed that this was the best exposure of hematite the rover had yet encountered. During this leg, Curiosity marked an impressive milestone, 2000 Martian days (or Sols) exploring Gale Crater! Looking southwest along Vera Rubin Ridge toward foothills of Mt Sharp. Credit NASA / JPL-Caltech / MSSS / Sean Doran

stops.name: InSight Landing Site
stops.text: InSight’s Landing Site: Elysium Planitia Looking eastward across the planned area for Mars InSight’s landing. InSight's landing site is Elysium Planitia, a flat, smooth plain selected not for its surface features, but for safety considerations. InSight's purpose is to study the interior of Mars, not the surface. Thus, in the selection of a landing site, what's on the surface mattered less on this mission than for previous rover missions focused on the geology. Planitia is Latin for a flat surface, geometric plane or flatness or a plain. Elysium is from the ancient Greek name for an afterlife paradise, usually referred to in English as the Elysian Fields. The landing site lies in the western portion of Elysium Planitia, centered at about 4.5 degrees north latitude and 135.9 degrees east longitude. This is just 373 miles (600 kilometers) from Curiosity’s landing site, Gale Crater. InSight takes 360-panoramic images in all directions at this landing site. Scientists expect a flat surface, no hills nearby and few large rocks in view. That is based on high-resolution images taken from orbit as part of thorough evaluations for selecting the site. The Landing Ellipse Landing ellipse for Mars InSight. Prior to touching down on Mars, the landing site for this mission is defined not as a point, but as a landing ellipse. The ellipse is about 81 miles (130 kilometers) long, generally west

stops.name: InSight Lander
stops.text: InSight Lander The view from MRO clearly shows the InSight lander on the surface of Mars. The lander shows up as a bright spot with the two darker solar power arrays extending to the left and right of the lander. The lander’s final rocket-powered descent disturbed dust around the landing site as can be seen by the darkened surface around the lander. In addition to a number of cameras, InSight’s scientific instruments include the Heat Flow and Physical Properties Package (HP3) provided by the German Aerospace Agency (DLR), the Seismic Experiment for Interior Structure (SEIS) provided by the French Space Agency (CNES), the Rotation and Interior Structure Experiment (RISE) led by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), the Temperature and Winds for InSight (TWINS) fabricated by the Spanish Astrobiology Center, and the Laser RetroReflector for InSight (LaRRI) provided by the Italian Space Agency. InSight Lander on Mars from MRO

stops.name: InSight Heat Shield
stops.text: Insight’s heat shield being attached to the aeroshell InSight’s aeroshell provided protection for the lander during its entry into Mars’ atmosphere. The aeroshell consisted of two parts, the backshell and the heat shield. The heat shield protected the lander from the intense heat (2,700 degrees Fahrenheit or 1,500 degrees Celsius) of entry into Mars’ atmosphere at 12,300 miles per hour (5.5 kilometers per second) and provided frictional braking. The heat shield was jettisoned when the lander slowed and got low enough to continue it’s descent by parachute. The heat shield can be seen on the surface of Mars from orbit by MRO. The shield fell about 757 meters to the northeast of the lander and apparently has its dark outside facing down. InSight heat shield on Mars from MRO

stops.name: InSight Backshell with Parachute
stops.text: Insight’s backshell being attached to InSight lander InSight’s aeroshell provided protection for the lander during its entry into Mars’ atmosphere. The aeroshell consisted of two parts, the backshell and the heat shield. As it approached and entered the atmosphere, thrusters on the backshell controlled the attitude of the aeroshell In addition to the frictional braking from the heat shield, the aeroshell’s angle of attack provided lift which helped slow the spacecraft’s descent. After this initial phase of descent, InSight jettisoned its heat shield and deployed a parachute from the backshell at a speed of 861 mph (385 meters per second) and an altitude of about 36,400 feet (11,100 meters) above the surface. The backshell and parachute were jettisoned once InSight had slowed to a speed of about 134 mph (60 meters per second) and descended to an altitude of 3,600 feet (1,100 meters). From there, InSight completed its descent using its 12 descent rocket engines. The heat shield can be seen on the surface of Mars from orbit by MRO. The backshell and parachute fell about 550 meters to the southeast of the lander. InSight backshell and parachute on Mars from MRO
